name: Herat
info: Herat is a city in western Afghanistan, in the valley of the Hari River, known in antiquity as Haraiva, a centre of Khorasan, the capital of the Timurids under Shah Rukh and Husayn Bayqara, and today the capital of Herat Province.

facts.founded: The precise date of foundation is unknown. The city is first recorded under the Achaemenid Empire (550 to 330 BCE), when the district was called Haraiva. The 14th-century writer Hamdallah Mustawfi said that a chief named Herat, a follower of the hero Nariman, first founded it, and that Alexander the Great rebuilt it after it had fallen to ruin.
facts.where: South of the Paropamisus Mountains, in the fertile valley of the Hari River, in western Afghanistan, on the roads to Iran and Turkmenistan.
facts.known: The Achaemenid district of Haraiva; Alexander's Artacoana; the Ghurid great mosque of 1201; the two Mongol sieges; the Kartid dynasty; the Timurid capital of Shah Rukh and Husayn Bayqara; the Musalla Complex; the poet and statesman Mir Ali-Shir Nava'i; the painter Behzad
facts.today: Herat is the capital of Herat Province and the third-largest city of Afghanistan, with an estimated 673,273 settled residents.

t: Herat was first recorded under the Achaemenid Empire as the chief town of the district of Haraiva, and it passed to Alexander, the Parthian and Sasanian empires, the Arabs, the Saffarids, the Samanids, the Ghaznavids, the Seljuk Empire, the Ghurids and the Khwarazm Empire.

The Mongols besieged it twice, in the second siege ending its life as a great city for a time, and under the Timurids, above all Shah Rukh and Husayn Bayqara, it became the capital of an empire and a centre of art and learning.
After the Safavids it was ruled by Afghan tribes, was independent for a time in the 19th century, was attacked by Iran several times, and was joined to Afghanistan in 1863.
dyk: In 1979 Herat had about 140,000 people, and today it has an estimated 673,273 settled residents.
ev: Alexander the Great captures the Arian capital, Artacoana, and rebuilds the town and builds the citadel
Hephthalites and Turks fight the Arab forces in the battle of Qohestan and are defeated

The Abdali Afghans of the city revolt and found the Sadozai Sultanate of Herat

sections.origins:
Herat lies south of the Paropamisus Mountains in the fertile valley of the Hari River, in western Afghanistan. It is first recorded in ancient times, but the date of its foundation is unknown. Under the Achaemenid Empire (550 to 330 BCE) the surrounding district was known by the Old Persian name Haraiva, and classical sources called the region Areia, or Aria. The Zoroastrian Avesta names the district Haroiva. The names of the district and of its chief town come from that of the local river, which was called Harayu in Old Iranian, a word that means "with velocity". Naming a region and its main town after the river was common in this part of the world.

The Achaemenid inscriptions list the district among the provinces, for example in the Behistun inscription of Darius I, dated to about 520 BCE, and men from it are shown in the reliefs at Naqsh-e Rustam and Persepolis, wearing Scythian-style dress with a tunic, trousers tucked into high boots and a twisted hood. In the 14th century Hamdallah Mustawfi wrote that a chief named Herat, one of the followers of the hero Nariman, first founded the city, and that Alexander the Great rebuilt it after it had fallen to ruin, with walls 9,000 paces round. In late 330 BCE Alexander captured the Arian capital, which was called Artacoana. The town was rebuilt and the citadel was constructed.
sections.growth:
Herat was a trading centre on routes from the Mediterranean to India and China, and geographers of the Abbasid period noted its textiles. In the 10th century Estakhri and Ibn Hawqal described a prosperous town with strong walls, many sources of water, extensive suburbs, an inner citadel, a congregational mosque and four gates, each opening on a market. The government building stood about a mile outside the city at Khorasanabad. A church was still visible in the countryside to the north-east, and a fire temple stood on a hilltop farther away.

Mustawfi wrote that Herat flourished especially under the Ghurids in the 12th century. He reported 359 colleges, 12,000 shops all occupied, 6,000 bath-houses, caravanserais, mills, a dervish convent and a fire temple, and about 444,000 houses with a settled population. The great mosque was built by Ghiyasuddin Ghori in 1201, and the city was a centre for metal goods, especially bronze with inlays of precious metals.

The city reached its greatest glory under the Timurid princes, especially Sultan Husayn Bayqara, who ruled it from 1469 until 4 May 1506. Shah Rukh, the youngest son of Timur, had been named governor in 1397 and encouraged building, manufacturing and trade, restoring and enlarging the bazaar. The Musalla Complex, the madrasa of Gawhar Shad and many gardens date from this time. The period was one of relative stability, prosperity and cultural activity.
sections.rulers:
Herat was part of the Achaemenid Empire and then fell to Alexander. It became part of the Seleucid Empire, and passed to the Parthian Empire in 167 BCE. In the Sasanian period (226 to 652 CE) it was one of the empire's provincial capitals, and in the last two centuries of Sasanian rule it was of great strategic importance in the wars between the Sasanians, the Chionites and the Hephthalites. The Arab armies appeared in Khorasan in the 650s, and Herat submitted and received an Arab governor, though like many places in Khorasan it rebelled and was reconquered several times. By 659 to 661 Tang China claimed a tenuous suzerainty over it, until local Turkish tribes drove the Tang out in 665.

Ya'qub ibn al-Layth al-Saffar took Herat in the 860s and 870s, and the Saffarids expelled the Taherids from Khorasan in 873. The Samanids ruled it for about a century, and their power was destroyed in 999 by the Qarakhanids and the Ghaznavids. Herat was captured by the Seljuk Empire in 1040, by the Ghurids in 1175 and by the Khwarazm Empire in 1214. After the Mongols, a local prince, Shams al-Din Kart, was named ruler in 1244 and confirmed by Hulagu in 1255, and his Kartid dynasty ruled until Timur took the city in 1380.

The Uzbeks occupied Herat in 1507, and Shah Isma'il of the Safavids took it in 1510. The Uzbeks held it again after his death until Shah Tahmasp retook it in 1528. Under the Safavids it was a provincial capital, and in the 16th century every Safavid ruler from Tahmasp I to Abbas I was governor of Herat in his youth. By the early 18th century the Abdali Afghans governed it.
sections.life:
Most sources suggest that Herat was predominantly Zoroastrian in the centuries before Islam. Around 430 it had a Christian community with a bishop of the Church of the East. Under the Arabs, hastily converted peoples elsewhere returned to their old beliefs once the armies had passed, and Herat itself was the scene of conflicts between different groups of Muslims and Arab tribes in the years before the Abbasid Caliphate, and a centre of the followers of Ustadh Sis. In the 12th century, according to Mustawfi, the men were Sunni Muslims who carried arms.

Herat produced learned men, among them the 11th-century mystic and poet Khwajah Abdullah Ansari, whose tomb at the village of Gazar Gah was first rebuilt by Shah Rukh about 1425 and became a shrine with other famous men buried around it. Under the Timurids the court was known for its sumptuous life, its music and its miniature painting. The vizier Mir Ali-Shir Nava'i, a poet and author in Persian and Turkish, was a great builder and patron of the arts, and the poet Jami and the painter Behzad also belonged to the city's history. The city had a Jewish community, with about 280 families in 1948, most of whom moved to Israel that year. The community had disappeared by 1992, and four former synagogues survive in the old quarter.

Most people in Herat speak Dari, a form of Persian, and Pashto is the second major language. Tajiks form the majority of the population.
sections.crises:
The Mongol Empire besieged Herat twice. The first siege ended in the surrender of the city, the slaughter of the local sultan's army of 12,000, and the appointment of two governors, one Mongol and one Muslim. The second was prompted by a rebellion against Mongol rule and lasted seven months, ending in June 1222. According to one account, the Mongols beheaded the entire population of 1,600,000, such that no head was left on a body and no body had a head. The city remained in ruins from 1222 to about 1236.

In 1793 Herat became independent for several years during the civil war among the sons of Timur Shah. The Iranians fought wars with Herat between 1801 and 1837, in 1804, 1807, 1811, 1814, 1817, 1818, 1821, 1822, 1825 and 1833, and besieged the city in 1837, when the British helped the Heratis repel them. In 1856 the Iranians invaded again and briefly took the city on 25 October, which led directly to the Anglo-Persian War. During the Panjdeh incident, the Musalla of Gawhar Shad was dynamited to keep the advancing Russian forces from using it.

In March 1979 the Afghan Army in Herat under Ismail Khan mutinied and protesters rose against the Khalq government; the rebels held the city for three days. Reprisals followed, and between 3,000 and 24,000 people, according to different sources, were killed. In April 1983 Soviet bombings damaged half of the city and killed an estimated 3,000 civilians. The Taliban captured the city on 5 September 1995 without much resistance, and put down a rebellion there in May 1999.
sections.legacy:
Herat was called the pearl of Khorasan, and the poet Rumi wrote of it as the pearl in the middle of the oyster of that province. After Timur's conquest it became an important centre of intellectual and artistic life in the Islamic world, and under Shah Rukh and Husayn Bayqara it was the focal point of the Timurid Renaissance, whose grandeur is thought to have matched that of Florence. In Safavid texts it was called the greatest of the cities of Iran, and Shah Abbas the Great was born there.

The city holds the Great Mosque, built by Ghiyasuddin Ghori in 1201, the citadel, called Qala Ikhtyaruddin or the Arg, and the Musalla Complex. Of the more than a dozen minarets that once stood in the city, many have been toppled by war and neglect during the past century, and UNESCO personnel and Afghan authorities have worked to stabilise the Fifth Minaret. The tomb of Dost Muhammad Khan, founder of the Barakzai dynasty, is in the city.

Afghanistan conquered Herat on 26 May 1863 under Dost Muhammad Khan, two weeks before his death, and it has been part of Afghanistan since. Herat fell to the Taliban on 12 August 2021. It is the capital of Herat Province and the third-largest city of Afghanistan.

summary: Herat, in the Hari River valley of western Afghanistan, was an Achaemenid district town, a Ghurid city and the seat of the Kartid dynasty, and under the Timurids the capital of an empire and a centre of art. It joined Afghanistan in 1863 and is its third-largest city.
notes: Only wp/herat.txt exists; no history article was available.
START: the article gives no foundation date ("precise date of foundation is unknown"); I used -550 with circa true, the start of the Achaemenid period in which it is first recorded.
The Achaemenid dates are given as 550-330 BC in the article; the Behistun date is 'ca. 520 BC'.
Tang suzerainty: the article says 659-661 and a rising in 665; I kept 'by 659 to 661' as 'tenuous'.
Saffarid dates: the article gives 870 (conquest), 861/862 raids, capture on 16 August 867 and again 872, and expulsion of Taherids 873; I wrote 860s and 870s rather than choosing one.

Mongol sieges: the article gives no year for the first; the second ended June 1222. My event label '1222' uses that. The 1,600,000 figure is given only as 'according to one account'. The article's population claim is implausible but is attributed.
Mustawfi's figures (359 colleges, 12,000 shops, 6,000 bath-houses, 444,000 houses) are his, attributed. The article's text puts them under the Ghurids.

The Timurid-era Islamic sources: the article says the tomb of Ansari was 'first rebuilt by Shahrokh about 1425'. Jami, Behzad: mentioned only from the notable-people list ('Persian Sufi poet of the 15th century', 'greatest of the medieval Persian painters'); I wrote only that they belonged to the city's history without giving more.
The article names Shah Isma'il's capture as 1510 and the Safavid retaking in 1528; 'In the 16th century ... governors in their youth' is as given.

Abdali revolt of 1716 appears only in the lead; the modern-history section says 'by the early 18th century Herat was governed by the Abdali Afghans', and the lead says the city became part of Afsharid Iran in 1732 (left out of the text but not contradicted). The Sadozai Sultanate of Herat is in the lead only.
1793 independence and the 1801-1837 wars are as stated. The lead says Herat was an independent city-state in the first half of the 19th century.
The article calls the Musalla destruction 'during the Panjdeh incident' without a date; I gave none (the incident is not dated there).

The article attributes the Herat 1979 reprisals killed 3,000-24,000 'according to different sources'; the 1983 bombing figure 3,000 is 'an estimated'. The Taliban's 1995 and 1999 events are bare dated facts; I left out the article's remarks on their laws and on the Heratis' character.

Left out: tourism, hotels, airport, rail, roads, sports, economy, sister city, mayor, the Hippie trail (a lasting fact but left for space), the 2001 and later events beyond the Taliban entry in 2021, the 'UNESCO World Heritage' announcement of 2021, 'customs revenue', ethnic percentages from 2003, and the modern people list except as noted.
The dyk uses two population figures from the article (1979 'around 140,000' and 'estimated 673,273'); the article gives no year for the second.
The 'life' section's sentence on Arab-era faith: the article quotes N. Dupree on hasty conversions in the east and in the mountains, not Herat specifically; I attributed it only to 'elsewhere'.
The article gives Mongol governor in 1244 as 'Mongol governor of Khorasan' naming Shams al-Din Kart; kept.
The article's section on ethnicity cites a 2003 National Geographic map; I wrote only that Tajiks form the majority, which the article states in its own voice.
